narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 61.9% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your first-year grades had the strongest influence. You placed in the second decile of your class, far below the average of sixth decile among accepted students. This low ranking strongly pushed the model toward expecting bar exam failure.

Your LSAT score of 35 was the second most important factor. Although this score is only slightly below the 37.2 average of accepted students, it still nudged the prediction slightly toward passing. However, this positive effect was not large enough to overcome the other signals.

Your family income bracket (middle) ranked third. This characteristic also increased the predicted chance of failure relative to students from higher-income families.

In short, the model concluded that your relatively weak first-year academic performance, combined with a middle-income background, outweighed the modest positive signal from your LSAT. 

What you should do next is focus on strengthening your academic record. Improving your grades in the coming years, retaking the LSAT if possible, or gaining additional relevant experience could meaningfully change how a future application is evaluated.
